words.context: A greeting. “Aye, yourself?” closes it. “How’s it gaun?” is the Scots version and means the same.
Universal. “Ta” works. “Cheers, aye” is the fuller and warmer version.
“Cheerio” is still current here in a way it isn’t in England. “Mind how you go” is the warm version.
Works for apologising and for getting past. The same reflex as England, deployed slightly less often.
Bar service by eye contact. Edinburgh bars are orderly and the barman is tracking who came in when.
Asking for “the check” marks you instantly.
Less common than in London and usually only for large groups. Read the bottom of the bill before tipping.
Tap on Lothian buses. If you pay cash they give no change at all, so bring the exact fare or use a card.
“Loo” works. Older pubs occasionally sign them in Scots or Gaelic with no English at all.

words.groupNote: Standard on most doors. “Fir” and “Mnathan” turn up on Gaelic signage — “Fir” is men.

words.context: Also “the hole in the wall.” Scottish banks issue their own notes, which are legal but sometimes refused in England.
Contactless everywhere. Say it as you hold the card up.
Scottish notes look nothing like Bank of England ones. Both work here; spend the Scottish ones before you leave.
Charged. Say “no thanks” if you brought one.
Gray, damp, cold, and endless — the specific Scottish weather that never quite commits to being rain.
Small, and also a softener attached to almost anything. “A wee minute” can comfortably mean an hour.
Know. “D’ye ken?” is “you know?” and “ah dinnae ken” is “I don’t know.”
A narrow covered passage off the Royal Mile leading to a courtyard. There are dozens and most are easy to walk straight past.
“Old Smoky” — Edinburgh’s own nickname, from the coal smoke that used to sit over the Old Town.
The groceries. “Away to get the messages” means going to the shops, and catches out every visitor once.
To chat at length about nothing in particular. Also a person who does rather too much of it.
“Go on yourself” — encouragement, approval, and open delight at someone doing well.
